name: Anonymity & Censorship Resistance
description: Anonymous communication (Tor, mix nets) and tools to detect or circumvent censorship.

ccs.narrative:
Anonymity and censorship resistance at CCS has been defined by the Tor ecosystem—fingerprinting attacks, flow correlation, and defenses—alongside global censorship measurement. Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning (CCS 2018) set a high-water mark by defeating every then-current Tor defense with a CNN. DeepCorr: Strong Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor Using Deep Learning (CCS 2018) showed flow correlation attacks could reliably deanonymize Tor users using deep learning on traffic patterns. Both papers drove a defensive research surge.

Defensive innovation followed: TrafficSliver: Fighting Website Fingerprinting Attacks with Traffic Splitting (CCS 2020) proposed routing Tor traffic across multiple entry guards to disrupt fingerprinting features. Measuring Information Leakage in Website Fingerprinting Attacks and Defenses (CCS 2018) provided an information-theoretic framework for evaluating these attacks quantitatively. Censored Planet: An Internet-wide, Longitudinal Censorship Observatory (CCS 2020) brought systematic measurement infrastructure to global censorship, tracking reachability across countries and protocols continuously.

By 2023, deep learning attack capability had grown further: Realistic Website Fingerprinting By Augmenting Network Traces (CCS 2023) made attacks more robust by augmenting training data, and Transformer-based Model for Multi-tab Website Fingerprinting Attack (CCS 2023) extended fingerprinting to multi-tab browsing scenarios. The community had not yet produced a defense that matched attacker pace.

ndss.narrative:
NDSS's treatment of anonymity and censorship resistance began with a focus on Tor measurement and traffic analysis. Inside Job: Applying Traffic Analysis to Measure Tor from Within (NDSS 2018) showed that middle relays can mount fingerprinting attacks from the inside, while early papers simultaneously tracked how censors were detecting and blocking circumvention proxies through protocol-level artifacts.

The 2019–2021 period widened the scope considerably. Papers examined how TLS is weaponized for censorship circumvention (The use of TLS in Censorship Circumvention, NDSS 2019), how state-level actors like Russia exercise decentralized control over the internet (Decentralized Control: A Case Study of Russia, NDSS 2020), and how automated discrepancy discovery (SymTCP, NDSS 2020) lets circumvention traffic evade deep packet inspection. Alongside these, metadata-hiding approaches for messaging and file sharing gained traction.

By 2023–2025 the community turned toward hardening anonymity systems at scale and exposing fresh infrastructure weaknesses. Wallbleed (NDSS 2025) disclosed a memory-disclosure vulnerability in the Great Firewall's DNS injection subsystem, and flow-correlation attacks on Tor onion services (Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor Onion Service Sessions with Sliding Subset Sum, NDSS 2024) demonstrated that deanonymization threats remain acute. Simultaneously, the search for practical mix-network designs and accountable anonymous broadcast produced protocols like Trellis and Ring of Gyges, reflecting a maturing effort to balance anonymity with abuse accountability.

milestones.title: Inside Job: Applying Traffic Analysis to Measure Tor from Within
milestones.note: Applies circuit and website fingerprinting from Tor middle relays to measure and deanonymize Tor traffic.

milestones.title: Cybercriminal Minds: An investigative study of cryptocurrency abuses in the Dark Web
milestones.note: Investigates cryptocurrency abuses on the Dark Web, linking illicit transactions and actors across underground channels.

milestones.title: Decentralized Control: A Case Study of Russia
milestones.note: This case study analyzes how Russia achieves decentralized Internet censorship without centralized technical choke-points.

milestones.title: Improving Signal's Sealed Sender
milestones.note: Identifies weaknesses in Signal's sealed-sender feature and proposes improved protocols for stronger sender anonymity.

milestones.title: Titanium: A Metadata-Hiding File-Sharing System with Malicious Security
milestones.note: Titanium is a metadata-hiding file-sharing system providing malicious security against compromised servers.

milestones.title: ProbFlow : Using Probabilistic Programming in Anonymous Communication Networks
milestones.note: Uses probabilistic programming to better estimate Tor relay capacities for anonymous communication networks.

milestones.title: Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor Onion Service Sessions with Sliding Subset Sum
milestones.note: Mounts effective flow correlation attacks on Tor onion service sessions using a sliding subset-sum technique.

milestones.title: Wallbleed: A Memory Disclosure Vulnerability in the Great Firewall of China
milestones.note: Discovers a buffer over-read memory disclosure vulnerability in the Great Firewall of China's DNS injection subsystem.

sp.narrative:
Anonymity research at IEEE S&P covers Tor traffic analysis, website fingerprinting, censorship measurement, and steganographic circumvention. Anonymity Trilemma: Strong Anonymity, Low Bandwidth Overhead, Low Latency - Choose Two (S&P 2018) provided a foundational impossibility result framing the design space for anonymous communication systems, showing that no protocol can simultaneously achieve all three properties.

The 2020 cohort combined attack and global measurement. High Precision Open-World Website Fingerprinting (S&P 2020) pushed traffic-analysis classifiers to the realistic open-world setting where the target page may not be in the training set. ICLab: A Global, Longitudinal Internet Censorship Measurement Platform (S&P 2020) deployed vantage points across dozens of countries to measure censorship consistently over years. Breaking and (Partially) Fixing Provably Secure Onion Routing (S&P 2020) found flaws in the security proofs for mix-net-style routing.

From 2021-2022, the Tor fingerprinting arms race intensified. Surakav: Generating Realistic Traces for a Strong Website Fingerprinting Defense (S&P 2022) synthesized realistic traffic patterns as a fingerprinting defense. DeepCoFFEA: Improved Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor via Metric Learning and Amplification (S&P 2022) improved flow-correlation attacks by pairing metric learning with statistical amplification. Defensive Technology Use by Political Activists During the Sudanese Revolution (S&P 2021) grounded these technical debates in real-world activist usage.

Robust Multi-tab Website Fingerprinting Attacks in the Wild (S&P 2023) and SoK: A Critical Evaluation of Efficient Website Fingerprinting Defenses (S&P 2023) jointly reassessed the state of the arms race, finding that many defenses fail in realistic multi-tab scenarios, while Discop: Provably Secure Steganography in Practice (S&P 2023) advanced censorship circumvention via distribution-preserving steganography.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this set, all from USENIX Security 2018, map out the core tensions of anonymity and censorship resistance. Some probe whether privacy tools deliver on their promises: "An Empirical Analysis of Anonymity in Zcash" (USENIX 2018) showed that Zcash's much-touted anonymity often collapses in practice once usage heuristics are applied, while "How Do Tor Users Interact With Onion Services?" (USENIX 2018) studied the usability gap that undermines anonymity in the wild. Others turned outward to the censor: "Quack: Scalable Remote Measurement of Application-Layer Censorship" (USENIX 2018) pushed censorship measurement past DNS- and IP-blocking to the application layer at global scale, and "Effective Detection of Multimedia Protocol Tunneling using Machine Learning" (USENIX 2018) signaled an emerging theme — that machine learning would become the censor's and the analyst's sharpest tool. Performance and resilience of Tor itself were also on the agenda, from circuit prediction to the bandwidth denial-of-service study "Point Break" (USENIX 2019).

Around 2020-2021 the field's center of gravity shifted toward website fingerprinting (WF) and the adversarial machine-learning arms race it spawned. "Zero-delay Lightweight Defenses against Website Fingerprinting" (USENIX 2020) sought practical defenses that did not destroy Tor's performance, and "Defeating DNN-Based Traffic Analysis Systems in Real-Time With Blind Adversarial Perturbations" (USENIX 2021) reframed both fingerprinting and flow correlation as a deep-learning game where adversarial perturbations could blind the classifier. In parallel, censorship circumvention matured into infrastructure-level evasion: "Balboa" (USENIX 2021) tunneled traffic through real application streams, and "Domain Shadowing" (USENIX 2021) repurposed CDNs for blocking-resistant communication. The community also grew more rigorous and more human-centered, with "Once is Never Enough" (USENIX 2021) establishing sound statistical foundations for Tor experimentation and "Collective Information Security in Large-Scale Urban Protests" (USENIX 2021) grounding the threat model in the lived experience of Hong Kong protesters.

By 2022-2023 the WF arms race intensified — "Online Website Fingerprinting" (USENIX 2022) stress-tested attacks under realistic conditions, and "Subverting Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Robust Traffic Representation" (USENIX 2023) showed defenses still falling to better feature representations. Measurement work sharpened on the censor's machinery, with "Many Roads Lead To Rome" (USENIX 2022) exposing how packet-header choices bias DNS censorship measurement and the landmark "How the Great Firewall of China Detects and Blocks Fully Encrypted Traffic" (USENIX 2023) reverse-engineering exactly how the GFW flags fully-encrypted protocols — directly informing the next generation of obfuscation. Automated and detection-resistant evasion arrived via "GET /out" (USENIX 2022) and "DeResistor" (USENIX 2023).

The most recent USENIX 2024-2025 papers show a field that is simultaneously consolidating and pushing toward provable guarantees. "Snowflake" (USENIX 2024) documented a deployed, ultra-light WebRTC-proxy circumvention system serving real users, while "SpotProxy" (USENIX 2024) tackled the economics of hosting proxies, and "Bridging Barriers" (USENIX 2024) surveyed the whole circumvention-tool ecosystem and its priorities. The cat-and-mouse continues — "Fingerprinting Obfuscated Proxy Traffic with Encapsulated TLS Handshakes" (USENIX 2024) shows obfuscation remains attackable — but "A Framework for Designing Provably Secure Steganography" (USENIX 2025) marks an aspiration to move beyond heuristic obfuscation toward formal, provable undetectability, suggesting where the area is headed next.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list reflects the two enduring battlefronts of anonymity research: deanonymizing Tor traffic, and measuring or evading censorship. On the attack side, 2018 marked a deep-learning inflection point. "Deep Fingerprinting: Undermining Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Deep Learning" (CCS 2018) showed that convolutional networks could classify which website a Tor user visited even against then-current defenses, while "DeepCorr: Strong Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor Using Deep Learning" (CCS 2018) brought the same machinery to end-to-end flow correlation. Alongside these, theory work like "Anonymity Trilemma: Strong Anonymity, Low Bandwidth Overhead, Low Latency - Choose Two" (S&P 2018) framed the fundamental limits any anonymity system must trade against, and "An Empirical Analysis of Anonymity in Zcash" (USENIX 2018) extended anonymity scrutiny to cryptocurrencies. On the censorship side, "Quack: Scalable Remote Measurement of Application-Layer Censorship" (USENIX 2018) began the push toward global, remote measurement.

Two parallel arms races then accelerated. For website fingerprinting (WF), attacks grew more practical: "Triplet Fingerprinting" (CCS 2019) used few-shot learning to make attacks portable across time, and defenders responded with "Zero-delay Lightweight Defenses against Website Fingerprinting" (USENIX 2020) and "TrafficSliver: Fighting Website Fingerprinting Attacks with Traffic Splitting" (CCS 2020). The community also grew more rigorous about realism and measurement, with "High Precision Open-World Website Fingerprinting" (S&P 2020) and later "Online Website Fingerprinting" (USENIX 2022) stress-testing whether lab results survive the real world. Meanwhile censorship research industrialized into continuous observatories: "Censored Planet: An Internet-wide, Longitudinal Censorship Observatory" (CCS 2020) and "ICLab: A Global, Longitudinal Internet Censorship Measurement Platform" (S&P 2020) turned one-off studies into ongoing global monitoring, and "Geneva: Evolving Censorship Evasion Strategies" (CCS 2019) automated the discovery of packet-manipulation evasions that previously took human experts.

By the early 2020s the field matured into a tightly coupled measure-countermeasure loop. Flow correlation kept advancing with "DeepCoFFEA: Improved Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor via Metric Learning and Amplification" (S&P 2022), while defenders explored generative traces in "Surakav: Generating Realistic Traces for a Strong Website Fingerprinting Defense" (S&P 2022) and adversarial perturbations in "Defeating DNN-Based Traffic Analysis Systems in Real-Time With Blind Adversarial Perturbations" (USENIX 2021). The threat model also expanded beyond single pages to messy real conditions, with multi-tab attacks ("Robust Multi-tab Website Fingerprinting Attacks in the Wild", S&P 2023) and trace augmentation ("Realistic Website Fingerprinting By Augmenting Network Traces", CCS 2023). On censorship circumvention, attention shifted to how nation-state firewalls actually behave, culminating in "How the Great Firewall of China Detects and Blocks Fully Encrypted Traffic" (USENIX 2023).

Where the area stands now is reflective and adversarially robust. Systematization work like "SoK: A Critical Evaluation of Efficient Website Fingerprinting Defenses" (S&P 2023) pushed the community to honestly assess which defenses actually hold, even as new attacks ("Subverting Website Fingerprinting Defenses with Robust Traffic Representation", USENIX 2023; "Robust and Reliable Early-Stage Website Fingerprinting Attacks", CCS 2024) keep raising the bar. The throughline across these venues is that deep learning made both deanonymization and evasion dramatically stronger, and the open frontier is durability under realistic, evolving conditions rather than idealized lab benchmarks.
